opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly I think the barrier is a lot lower than people assume. A lot of ML engineers look at science and think, "I'd need a PhD in chemistry or physics before I can contribute anything." But the truth is, many of the hardest problems in AI for science right now are actually machine learning and engineering problems. How do you build models that respect symmetries? How do you scale training on huge molecular datasets? How do you build good data pipelines, good benchmarks, good infrastructure for running simulations alongside learned models? Those are things practitioners already know how to do very well.

So my first piece of advice would be: just start somewhere concrete. Pick a problem area that excites you. Maybe it's materials for carbon capture, maybe it's drug discovery, maybe it's climate or weather modeling. Then find an open dataset and an open benchmark. There are quite a few of them now, things around molecular property prediction, protein structure, catalysts. Download the data, run a baseline, and try to beat it. You'll learn the domain language very quickly that way, because you'll be forced to understand what the inputs and outputs actually mean.

The second thing is: find a collaborator who is a domain scientist. That's really where the magic happens. The scientist knows which questions actually matter and where the current tools fail, and you bring the ability to build models that scale and actually work in practice. These teams of two very different kinds of people are, I think, the most productive unit in this field. And scientists are generally very happy to talk to people who can build things, so don't be shy about reaching out.

Third, learn a bit of the fundamentals, but in a targeted way. You don't need to become a quantum chemist, but understanding a bit about things like equivariance, why physical systems have symmetries, what a simulation is actually computing, what density functional theory roughly does, that goes a long way. Many of the tools we use in deep learning, like graph neural networks, diffusion models, and generative modeling in general, map really naturally onto these problems once you see the structure.

And finally, I'd say keep in mind that in science the loop doesn't close in the computer. At some point somebody has to go into the lab and make the molecule or the material and test it. So if you can, get involved with projects that actually connect to experiments, because that's where you really learn what matters. A model that looks great on a benchmark but fails in the lab isn't very useful, and that feedback is incredibly educational.

So to summarize: the skills you have are already very valuable. Pick a problem you care about, find a scientist to work with, learn just enough of the domain, and try to connect to the real world. I think this is one of the most exciting places to be right now, because the impact on things like climate, energy, and health can be enormous.

r001.rationale: The response advises practitioners to start with a concrete problem, dataset, and benchmark, but does not propose beginning workshops with an introductory tutorial for newcomers.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thank you for having me. I think the first thing I'd say is that the barrier is lower than people assume. A lot of what makes AI for science hard isn't the machine learning, it's the science. And the good news is that scientists are generally quite eager to collaborate, because they have problems that they know are solvable with modern tools but they don't have the engineering skills or the time to build those tools themselves. So if you're a practitioner, the single most valuable thing you can do is find a scientist and talk to them. Go to a university, go to a seminar, join a reading group. Ask them what their bottleneck is. Very often it's something mundane from an ML perspective, like a pipeline that's too slow, or a model that doesn't generalize, or data that's noisy and they don't know how to handle that, and you can make a real contribution there without being an expert in chemistry or biology.

The second thing I'd say is pick a domain and go reasonably deep. You don't need a PhD, but you do need to understand the basic physics or chemistry of the problem, because otherwise you'll build models that violate the constraints of the system, and the scientists will not trust you. If you want to work on molecules, learn what a force field is, learn what density functional theory computes, learn why equivariance to rotations matters. That's maybe a few months of reading, and it pays off enormously, because then you can have a real conversation about what the model should and should not do.

And then the third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that there's a lot of open infrastructure now. There are datasets like the Open Catalyst Project or the various protein structure datasets, there are benchmark tasks, there are open-source libraries for geometric deep learning and for simulation. So you can actually get your hands dirty from home. You can train a model on a materials dataset over a weekend and see what happens. That's a very different situation from ten years ago, when you needed to be inside a lab with access to proprietary data.

I'd also say don't underestimate the value of your engineering skills. Science has a reproducibility problem, and a lot of scientific code is, frankly, not very good. Someone who knows how to write tests, how to version data, how to build a clean training loop, how to scale something to a GPU cluster, that person is incredibly valuable in a scientific group. You may feel like you're doing plumbing, but the plumbing is often what determines whether the science gets done.

And the final thing is to be a bit humble and a bit patient. Scientists have been thinking about these problems for a long time, and the easy problems have usually been solved already. When a scientist tells you something won't work, it's worth listening, because there's usually a good physical reason. But equally, they're often wrong about what ML can do, because the field has moved so fast. So the sweet spot is somebody who listens carefully but also pushes back with concrete experiments. If you can do that, you'll be in demand, and I genuinely believe that this is where some of the most impactful work of the next decade is going to happen.

r001.rationale: The response advises practitioners to contact scientists, study a domain, use open infrastructure, and contribute engineering skills. It does not propose starting AI-for-science workshops with an introductory tutorial.

astra-6.text:
I think the best way is to find a scientist to collaborate with. If you’re an AI practitioner, you have skills that are very useful, but you need somebody who understands the scientific question and the data. What are we trying to measure? What would constitute an interesting discovery? Where could the data be misleading?

And I would start with a concrete, relatively small problem. A lot of scientific work involves processing data, building models, and running expensive simulations. You might help automate an analysis or build a surrogate model that makes a simulation faster. That can be enormously valuable, even if it doesn’t involve inventing a new machine-learning method.

The interesting part is the exchange. You learn enough about the science to understand why your model needs certain constraints, and the scientist learns what machine learning can offer. You don’t have to become an expert in the entire discipline before you can contribute, but you do have to be curious and willing to learn its language.

r001.rationale: The response recommends collaborating with a scientist and starting with a small problem; it does not propose workshops or an introductory tutorial for newcomers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the best way is to team up with a scientist who has a concrete problem. You don’t have to become a physicist or a chemist before you can contribute. There are many scientists who have data and interesting questions, but who don’t have the expertise to build the machine learning tools themselves. As an AI practitioner, you can bring something very valuable to that collaboration.

But you do need to be curious about the science. Spend time understanding what they’re trying to measure, what the limitations of the data are, and what would actually count as a useful result. Sometimes improving a prediction is valuable; sometimes the real bottleneck is deciding which experiment to do next.

So I would start small: find a research group, identify a problem together, and build something that helps them make progress. You learn the science through the collaboration, and they learn what AI can offer.

r001.rationale: The candidate recommends finding a research group and starting with a concrete problem. It does not propose beginning AI-for-science workshops with an introductory tutorial for newcomers.
